extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent prosecutors, and IP litigators working on AI/software inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting, prosecuting, and litigating patents for AI-related inventions, with emphasis on subject-matter eligibility (Alice), claim drafting for detectability, and enforcement strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-part subject-matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the two-step Alice/Mayo test: (1) determine whether claims are 'directed to' an abstract idea (e.g., mathematical concepts, mental processes, methods of organizing human activity); (2) if so, determine whether claim elements add an 'inventive concept' that transforms the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts often resolve §101 issues at early stages (motion to dismiss, judgment on the pleadings). Claims that recite only high-level functions performed by generic computing modules are vulnerable. In step two, an inventive concept requires more than well-understood, routine, conventional components or simply applying the abstract idea using generic computer technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite specific technical/AI elements or architecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that lack AI-specific elements or architecture (i.e., only describe high-level goals or outcomes) risk being found directed to abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the specification mentions neural networks or AI, courts have invalidated claims when the claim language itself does not require or recite those technical elements. Include concrete technical components or configurations in claims rather than generic 'modules' or functional language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe specific technical details of analysis in specification and claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide concrete, technical details about the exact sort of analysis, algorithms, or architecture rather than broad descriptions of data analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts criticized claims that covered 'history data analysis' broadly without technical specifics; lack of specific technical details can lead to preemption concerns and §101 invalidity. Where possible, claim and describe the particular technical steps or structures used to perform analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim an improvement to computer/technical field
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims to be directed to an actual improvement in computer architecture or another technical field (e.g., improved processor architecture or improved speech-recognition performance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have treated claimed improvements to computer architecture (e.g., LPHDR processing elements) as plausibly inventive and sufficient to survive early pleadings. The specification should explain how the invention improves the relevant technical field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid preempting broad methods or mental processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not claim concepts so broadly that they would preempt a general method of analyzing data or performing mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts invalidate claims whose breadth would effectively preempt all methods of performing a particular abstract idea. Tailor claim scope to technical implementations rather than abstract goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should recite a specific implementation comprising technical elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, ensure claims are tied to concrete implementations (technical elements, structures, or configurations) rather than abstract descriptions of functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB and courts have credited claims that recite technical elements (e.g., AI + computer speech recognition) as not 'directed to' an abstract idea. Specific implementation language in claims helps distinguish from abstract idea categorizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must show how the invention provides a technical improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification should explicitly describe how the claimed invention improves the technical field (performance, simplicity, accuracy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB relied on specification statements (e.g., improved performance using DeepSpeech learning) to find claims directed to a technical improvement. Emphasize empirical or technical advantages over prior art in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim detectable features (viewable when product is operated)
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft claims to include features that are visible or discernible when an AI-enabled product/method is operated (UI elements, outputs, intermediate results).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detectable features make enforcement feasible because infringement can be observed in product operation or user interfaces. Examples: UI prompting for inputs, displayed intermediate/final AI results, or user-specific criteria used for training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus claims on model/architecture elements likely disclosed in competitor materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Target model/architecture aspects (e.g., '7 layer neural network') that competitors may advertise or mention in marketing, allowing detection from public materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitor marketing or technical descriptions may overtly describe architecture to compete on features; capturing those elements in claims aids detection without reverse engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim commissioning/training/process features that appear in user guides/manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Include steps or features related to commissioning, setup, or training of AI systems, since such details may be present in user guides, technical manuals, or commissioning documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Products that require per-customer setup often document these steps; claiming them increases the chance infringement will be provable from publicly available documentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for cloud-based/aaS models limiting detectability from documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that cloud/aaS providers typically document only interaction points (APIs, UI), not internal implementation details, reducing detectability from public docs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When features are kept as provider-controlled trade secrets and only interaction interfaces are documented, infringement detection via documentation is harder. Consider claiming features observable at the client/edge or disclosed in customer-facing docs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design claims with the dataflow between edge and centralized compute in mind
rubrics_metrics.description: When inventions involve centralized/cloud compute and edge devices, draft claims targeting observable dataflow, edge-side processing, or callbacks ('call back home') that can reveal operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features solely inside centralized compute may be hard to detect; the after-effects or data transmitted to edge devices are often easier to observe and can serve as proxies for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider reverse-engineering feasibility for detection
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether infringing features can be reverse-engineered from deployed devices, recognizing that reverse engineering can expose inputs, pre-processing, feature engineering, and trained models at the edge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reverse engineering can detect otherwise hidden features but typically requires high effort and technical competence, making it unsuitable for casual analyses. Where reverse-engineering is feasible, claims can be drafted to capture those discoverable aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve non-detectable technical details as trade secrets when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: If certain implementation details will never be detectable and are critical to competitive advantage, consider keeping them as trade secrets rather than disclosing them in a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent practitioners should discuss with inventors which details are detectable and which are better kept secret; avoid disclosing non-detectable but commercially valuable details when trade secret protection is preferable and consistent with patentability requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim features that map to essential features of standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If patented technology corresponds to an essential feature of an industry standard, mapping claims to that essential feature simplifies infringement detection against standard-compliant products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards bodies may require FRAND/royalty-free licensing. Contributing technology to standards can be strategic. Essential features in standards are typically included in compliant products, easing infringement proof; optional features may require additional proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of whether claimed combinations are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional'
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the combination of claim elements, especially generic computer components, would be considered conventional as of the invention date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Alice step two, an inventive concept is not present if the only alleged innovation is applying an abstract idea using conventional components. Courts will examine whether the combination amounts to significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming purely functional/desirable results without concrete means
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely claim desirable outcomes or functions (e.g., 'optimize parameters') without concrete means or technical steps risk being characterized as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to recite how the desired result is achieved (structures, algorithms, data transformations) rather than only stating the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage USPTO examples and PEG guidance where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the USPTO 2019 PEG/MPEP examples as drafting guides; some examples illustrate patent-eligible AI claims (e.g., Example 39: two-stage neural network training to reduce false positives).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Align claim and specification drafting with examples that the USPTO has labeled patent-eligible to increase chances of passing examiner eligibility review; ensure claims avoid reciting mathematical concepts/mental processes when those are problematic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think broadly about the inference and datapoints to capture broader infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: When drafting claims, consider what the claimed inference represents and what datapoints could be substituted to perform the same inference, to capture broader infringement beyond a single productized embodiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different ML architectures can produce similar inferences; scope claims to cover the inference or effect (through concrete technical means) rather than only a single model embodiment so competitors can't easily design around by swapping datapoints or models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer claiming observable post-processing or user-facing consequences for cloud-only innovations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the novel computation happens only in the cloud, claim observable consequences, outputs, or interactions that are visible to users or clients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because provider-managed internal workings are often undisclosed, claiming client-visible artifacts, API behaviors, or edge-side effects makes enforcement achievable.
